title: Never Trust An LLM
summary: Matt Pocock makes the case that LLMs hallucinate constantly - factual errors, fabricated entities, and contextual inconsistencies - and that developers and anyone relying on extrinsic (training-data) knowledge should never trust them implicitly. He walks a taxonomy from an academic paper, with famous examples: Google's Bard advert confidently claiming the JWST took the first pictures of an exoplanet (Alphabet shares dropped 8%), LLMs inventing npm packages that open the door to supply-chain malware attacks, and the Air Canada chatbot that invented a bereavement-refund policy the airline was then liable for. He then explains why hallucination is structural rather than fixable: training is a lossy compression of the internet into GPU-sized weights, so the model holds only a blurry low-res version of knowledge, and - per an OpenAI paper - training and benchmark evaluation reward guessing over admitting uncertainty, because you miss all the shots you do not take. His practical defense: feed the model intrinsic information (documents, your codebase), and for anything you do not know, use the four-word prompt 'Use your search tool' so answers are grounded in fetched articles with citations - and still verify critical facts yourself.
what_you_learn: You get a working mental model of why LLMs hallucinate (lossy compression plus reward structures that favor confident guessing) and a concrete operating procedure: never rely on a model's training-data memory for facts, push information into its context or make it search and cite sources, and keep a human verification loop for anything critical. This is directly applicable to designing reliable AI-agent systems where hallucinated APIs, packages, or config values can silently break a build or worse.

skills.name: Hallucination Management
skills.description: Naming the distinct failure modes - factual errors, fabricated entities, contextual inconsistency - so you can spot and discuss them.

skills.name: System Prompt Design
skills.description: LLMs are far more reliable on information you send them in the conversation than on knowledge from their training data.

skills.name: Context Engineering
skills.description: Training compresses the internet lossily into weights, so models hold only a blurry low resolution copy of facts.

skills.name: AI Benchmarking
skills.description: Benchmarks and training reward guessing over refusing, so models are tuned to take shots rather than admit uncertainty.

skills.name: AI Output Verification
skills.description: For critical, legal, or health-related facts, read the source documents yourself even when the model searched.

learnings.title: Hallucinations come in distinct types, and developers get the worst one
learnings.detail: Matt references a comprehensive taxonomy of hallucinations in LLMs (arXiv 2508.01781). The first type is factual errors, present since the beginning: Google's Bard advert claimed the James Webb Space Telescope took the very first pictures of a planet outside our solar system - wrong, and Alphabet's share price dropped roughly 8% after posting. The developer-relevant type is fabricated entities: ask 'does a package exist for this purpose' and the LLM will very likely say yes, inventing packages that have burned Matt dozens of times and opening developers to supply-chain malware attacks via false recommendations. Models also invent government departments and laws.

learnings.title: Distinguish intrinsic from extrinsic information
learnings.detail: The paper's key distinction: intrinsic information is what you have sent the model in this conversation (tell it your cat is called Bandit, and it should answer from that); extrinsic information is everything in its training data (ask for your cat's name in a fresh chat and it should say it does not know). Hallucinating against provided context is an intrinsic hallucination; guessing from training data is extrinsic. Matt's experience: models are much, much more reliable when you send them the information first, and relying on extrinsic knowledge is where you get disappointed.

learnings.title: Contextual inconsistency: models can ignore what you explicitly gave them
learnings.detail: The third type is ignoring or contradicting context you explicitly provided. His example is the 2024 Air Canada case: Jake Moffatt asked the airline's chatbot about bereavement fares; even though the real policy was in the model's context, it invented a 90-day refund window. Air Canada was found liable for the chatbot's misleading advice. The takeaway is uncomfortable: even intrinsic, explicitly provided information can be overridden - which is why critical facts still need verification.

learnings.title: Training is lossy compression - that is the root cause
learnings.detail: Training takes a massive scraped training set and compresses it into weights small enough to fit on a GPU; the output is much smaller than the input, so information is lost. Matt's analogy: compress a photo of him step by step until he is a blobby person you can barely recognize. You can still answer coarse questions (what color is the microphone cap) but not precise ones (who is this, how old). A model's memory of anything outside its training data - or anything rare - is that blobby, hyper-compressed version of the original information.

learnings.title: Models guess because guessing is rewarded
learnings.detail: Per OpenAI's paper 'Why Language Models Hallucinate' (arXiv 2509.04664): like students facing hard exam questions, models guess when uncertain because training and evaluation procedures reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty. Benchmarks such as LiveBench score models out of 100, and a model tuned to say 'I don't know' scores worse than one that guesses - you miss all the shots you don't take. Matt frames the design tension in human terms: very smart people are rarely humble about it, and the people who train and grade LLMs must pick a point on that confidence line - he is not sure it is solvable.

learnings.title: The four-word prompt: Use your search tool
learnings.detail: For questions where you cannot supply the information, Matt's fix is the prompt 'Use your search tool'. Most agent harnesses - Claude included, via the web search connector he always keeps on - give the model a web search tool. Saying this forces the model to pull articles into its context and answer from those (ideally with citations, as in his Arsenal injury-list demo), converting an extrinsic question into an intrinsic one. The catch: a confident model may skip searching because it thinks it already knows, which is exactly the failure mode this prompt works around.

learnings.title: Grounded context is why AI coding works so well
learnings.detail: Matt is still strongly pro-LLM because when coding you naturally pass intrinsic information: the codebase, big files, documents. The model explores the code and gives genuinely good insights, far more accurate than recall-based answers. The general principle for agent systems: always make sure you are providing the information the model needs to succeed, rather than asking it to know things.

learnings.title: Verify the sources yourself for anything critical
learnings.detail: Even the search-tool fix has a hole: contextual inconsistency means even fetched or provided documents can be misread or ignored - the Air Canada chatbot is the extreme case. So for life-or-death, health, or especially legal questions, have the model search, then actually read the documents yourself. The same happens constantly in coding: an LLM misreads code and answers confidently, and you must correct it. Trust is a loop you keep closed, not a property of the model.

key_points: LLMs hallucinate constantly, and their confident delivery hides it - never trust them implicitly.
Intrinsic beats extrinsic: send the model the information and it becomes far more reliable.
An LLM's training-data memory is a blurry, over-compressed photo of the internet.
Benchmarks reward guessing over refusing, so models are trained to take every shot.
Never let an LLM recommend a package without verifying it exists - supply-chain malware is real.
The four-word prompt 'Use your search tool' converts recall questions into grounded ones.
Air Canada was legally liable for its chatbot's invented refund policy.
For critical facts, search is not enough - a human must read the sources.
